catalog_quote: El lacandón del norte presenta un patrón acentual trocaico (*.), en el cual el acento recae en la primera sílaba de una palabra bisilábica. ... El lacandón del sur y el yucateco presentan el mismo tipo de patrón acentual yámbico (.*), el cual se caracteriza porque el acento de una palabra bisilábica recae en la segunda sílaba ... En ambas lenguas la sílaba con mayor prominencia acentual es la sílaba final. Cabe mencionar que tanto en lacandón del norte, como en lacandón del sur y en yucateco las sílabas que se encuentran a final de palabra siempre son cerradas (CVC). (4) Acento final en lacandón del sur a. [pe.ˈpen] ‘mariposa b. [ku.ˈʃup] ‘epazote’ c. [pet.ˈhɐʔ] ‘laguna’ ... el lacandón del sur y el yucateco presentan vocales largas. En este sentido, ambas lenguas son sensibles al peso silábico (Mojica Hernández, 2012). De tal manera que cuando aparece una vocal larga como núcleo de una sílaba no-final, el acento es atraído hacia la sílaba que contiene vocal larga o re-articulada, como se muestra en los ejemplos (6) y (7). En el caso del lacandón del sur, se observa que las sílabas con vocal larga, ejemplos (6a) y (6b), o rearticulada (6c), llevan el acento de palabra. ... (6) Acento en lacandón del sur a. [ˈk’ɐ:m.buɾ] ‘faisán’ b. [ˈmi:.sip] ‘escoba’ c. [ˈʧɐˀɐ.nɘɾ] ‘elote’ ... En cuanto al lacandón del norte, si bien no presenta vocales largas, el acento fijo siempre aparece en la primera sílaba de una palabra bisilábica.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.translation: Northern Lacandon (LN) shows a trochaic stress pattern (*.), in which stress falls on the first syllable of a bisyllabic word. | Southern Lacandon (LS) and Yucatec show the same iambic stress pattern (.*), characterised by the stress of a bisyllabic word falling on the second syllable. [...] In both languages the syllable with the greatest stress prominence is the final syllable. | both LS and Yucatec are languages sensitive to syllable weight (Mojica Hernández 2012), so that when a long vowel occurs as the nucleus of a non-final syllable, stress is attracted to the syllable containing the long or rearticulated vowel
new_statements.citation: Mojica Hernández, Liliana. 2014. Comparación sincrónica de los sistemas vocálicos del lacandón y el yucateco. MA thesis, Universidad Autónoma Metropolitana-Iztapalapa, México. doi:10.24275/uami.c534fn93r
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (extracted text of the 63-page UAM thesis PDF, text layer present, printed page numbers = PDF pages). All four quoted sentences are there verbatim: p. 47 §3.3.2 'El LN presenta un patrón acentual trocaico (*.), en el cual el acento recae en la primera sílaba de una palabra bisilábica' with (9) [ˈpe.pen] [ˈmi.sip] [ˈpet.hɐʔ]; p. 48 §3.3.3 'El LS y YUC presentan el mismo tipo de patrón acentual yámbico (.*), el cual se caracteriza porque el acento de una palabra bisilábica recae en la segunda sílaba.. En ambas lenguas la sílaba con mayor prominencia acentual es la sílaba final' with (10) [pe.ˈpen] [ku.ˈʃup] [pet.ˈhɐʔ]; p. 48 'tanto el LS como el YUC son lenguas sensibles al peso silábi…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Two systems under one glottocode. Southern Lacandon (Lacanjá Chansayab): stress on the final syllable by default; a non-final syllable with a long or rearticulated (laryngealized) vowel is heavy and takes the stress instead (e.g. [ˈmi.sip] 'broom', [ˈk’ɐ:m.buɾ] 'pheasant' vs [pe.ˈpen] 'butterfly', [to.ˈɾok] 'iguana'). Northern Lacandon (Nahá, Metzabok): no contrastive/phonetic vowel length in the young speakers studied and fixed stress on the first syllable of bisyllabic words ([ˈpe.pen], [ˈmi.sip], [ˈto.ɾok]). The reading 'weight-sensitive' is assigned for Southern Lacandon; Northern Lacandon would be 'fixed: initial syllable'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed in Mojica 2014. Bennett 2016 (p. 500) points to Herrera Zendejas 2014 Ch.10 for 'possible phonetic evidence of secondary stress in Lacandon' (not seen first-hand).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; data are bisyllabic (max. three-syllable) words elicited in isolation from word lists (2 LN speakers from Nahá, 2 LS speakers from Lacanjá Chansayab, ages 21-30). Author notes that LN word-final syllables are always closed (CVC) and that LN's apparent loss of vowel length may be a change in progress, so the LN fixed pattern is tentative (p. 59: 'puede implicar que esta lengua presente un patrón de acento fijo'). Southern Lacandon is also reported (Wikipedia citing Mojica & Martínez Corripio 2018; Bennett 2016 citing Canger 1995 ms.) to have high/low lexical tone on long vowels, which the thesis does not analyse.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms elicited in isolation ('palabras producidas de manera aislada'); acoustic (duration/formant) study, stress judged perceptually plus duration; no phrase-level statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog laca1243 'Lacandon' has no dialect children, but the source (Mojica Hernández 2014) treats Northern Lacandon (LN: Nahá and Metzabok, Ocosingo, Chiapas; ~200-250 speakers) and Southern Lacandon (LS: Lacanjá Chansayab; ~300-500 speakers) as separate languages with different stress systems: LN fixed initial (trochaic, bisyllables), LS final/weight-sensitive (iambic, like Yucatec). The 'weight-sensitive' reading is for Southern Lacandon, the variety also described by Hofling 2014 and Martínez Corripio 2018; Bruce 1968 and Bergqvist 2008 describe Northern Lacandon speakers. No separate glottocodes exist for the two varieties.

new_statements.translation: Southern Lacandon and Yucatec show the same type of iambic stress pattern (.*), characterized by the stress of a disyllabic word falling on the second syllable [...] In both languages the syllable with the greatest stress prominence is the final syllable. It should be noted that in Northern Lacandon, Southern Lacandon and Yucatec alike, word-final syllables are always closed (CVC). [...] both languages are sensitive to syllable weight (Mojica Hernández 2012). Thus, when a long vowel appears as the nucleus of a non-final syllable, stress is attracted to the syllable containing the long or rearticulated vowel [...] syllables with a long vowel, examples (6a) and (6b), or a rearticulated vowel (6c), carry the word stress.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement and same weight mechanism as the existing statement from the first author's 2014 UAM thesis (final stress in disyllables, attracted to a non-final syllable with a long or rearticulated vowel), now with acoustic data and journal pagination. The catalog record for laca1243 has an empty rule field; this article supplies the rule. The Northern Lacandon statements in the same article (trochaic, fixed initial stress, §5.3.1 p. 88 and p. 91) concern a different variety (Nahá/Metzabok), not the catalog's Southern Lacandon.
new_statements.rule_in_words: In Southern Lacandon (Lacanjá Chansayab) word stress is final by default in disyllables (final syllables are always closed CVC): [pe.ˈpen] 'butterfly', [ku.ˈʃup] 'epazote', [pet.ˈhɐʔ] 'lagoon', [to.ˈɾok] 'iguana'. A non-final syllable whose nucleus is a long vowel or a rearticulated (glottalized VʔV) vowel attracts the stress instead: [ˈk’ɐ:m.buɾ] 'pheasant', [ˈmi.sip] 'broom', [ˈʧɐˀɐ.nɘɾ] 'ear of corn'. The conclusions (p. 99) restate that in Southern Lacandon and Yucatec phonetic vowel length 'defines the position of word stress, since both languages are sensitive to syllable weight', whereas Northern Lacandon has fixed stress on the first syllable of a disyllable.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. The authors add (p. 93) that a proper syllabic analysis is still needed 'para determinar los tipos de acento' shown for the three languages, i.e. the stress typing is offered as provisional. Only disyllables are exemplified.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog laca1243 'Lacandon' (ISO lac) has dialect children Lacanjá (laca1244) and Najá; the catalog item is labelled Southern Lacandon. The 2018 article's Southern Lacandon data come from Lacanjá Chansayab, Chiapas (Table on p. 51: ~500 speakers), and its Northern Lacandon data from Nahá/Metzabok. The article warns (fn. 3, p. 52) that Northern Lacandon speakers living in Lacanjá Chansayab show contact features. Bruce 1968 is a grammar of the Najá (Northern) variety.

sources.note: Section 3.3 'Patrón acentual' (pp. 45-49) + conclusions p. 59: Northern Lacandon (Nahá/Metzabok) has a fixed trochaic pattern, stress on the first syllable of a bisyllabic word ([ˈpe.pen], [ˈmi.sip]); Southern Lacandon (Lacanjá Chansayab), like Yucatec, is iambic — stress on the final syllable ([pe.ˈpen], [pet.ˈhɐʔ]) — but weight-sensitive: a non-final syllable with a long or rearticulated (laryngealized) vowel attracts stress ([ˈk’ɐ:m.buɾ], [ˈmi.sip], [ˈʧɐˀɐ.nɘɾ]). Based on acoustic study of word-list elicitation from 2 LN and 2 LS speakers.
